content: Health workers should be proficient in utilizing cross-sectional reports for planning purposes. They must also understand how to use antiretroviral therapy (ART) cohort analysis reports to identify patient outcomes and ensure appropriate follow-up actions are taken. In addition to accurately completing all patient monitoring tools, health workers should be able to use the collected and reported data to inform both individual patient management and overall program monitoring at the healthcare facility. Each piece of information collected and every indicator measured serves a specific purpose. Therefore, data utilization should be conducted regularly and integrated as a routine part of delivering quality care and treatment. Quality assurance activities can be enhanced by reviewing some of the collected data. Regular site visits by district management teams and clinical mentors can further support health workers in effectively using data. It is essential for health workers to recognize that using data is just as important as collecting, entering, and reporting it. All relevant staff in maternal and child health (MCH) clinics should have received appropriate training on the national patient monitoring system within the past specified months. This includes doctors, clinical officers, nurses, nurse assistants, data clerks, lay counselors, and other specified personnel. If any relevant staff members have not been trained in one or more components of the patient monitoring system, the district team should schedule and provide appropriate training or retraining. This should be followed by hands-on support within 2–4 weeks. For infant monitoring, specific data points must be recorded, including the infant's age at the start of cotrimoxazole (CTX), HIV test date, age, type, and results, date of enrollment in HIV care/ART, unique ID number, ART start date, tuberculosis (TB) status, and final TB/HIV status. Similarly, all relevant staff in TB clinics should have received training on the national patient monitoring system within the past specified months. This includes doctors, clinical officers, nurses, nurse assistants, data clerks, lay counselors, and other specified personnel. If any staff members are not trained in one or more components of the patient monitoring system, the district team should arrange for appropriate training or retraining, followed by hands-on support within 2–4 weeks. The TB monitoring system should include key HIV-related elements such as HIV test dates and results, CPT start dates, ART start dates, ARV regimen details (including date and dose dispensed), unique ID numbers, CD4 test dates and results, viral load (VL) test dates and results, and antenatal care (ANC) numbers. If any of these elements are missing, the tools used should be listed and addressed. The final action plan emphasizes that the ART patient monitoring review (APMR) should not proceed if critical issues are identified during the initial assessment. These include the complete absence of HIV patient cards (or equivalent tools) or ART registers not being filled out at all. The APMR can proceed only if specific setting-relevant conditions are met.
